xref.title: John Lennon's Clash with Red Robinson (1964)
xref.body: Halfway through the Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, as the crowd neared rioting, local radio host Red Robinson was instructed to go on stage to calm the fans. John Lennon, unaware of the situation, confronted Robinson, telling him, "Get off our stage, nobody interrupts the Beatles," before relenting after Robinson explained that manager Brian Epstein had sent him. "John looked down at Brian Epstein, the band's manager who gave him the okay. John turned Robinson and said, Okay, carry on mate."

xref.title: Founder of CBGB (1973)
xref.body: Hilly Crystal, an ex-marine, opened the CBGB club in 1973 in the Bowery neighborhood of New York. Despite the area being an economic and social disaster zone at the time, the cheap rent allowed starving artists to live, rehearse, and create. Crystal established the club's musical policy, which fostered an environment where artists, "freaks, and weirdos" could do their own thing, leading to the birth of punk rock. "When an ex-marine named Hilly Crystal opened the place in 1973, it was in a part of town where nobody wanted to go."

xref.title: Early Label Rejection & Sire Signing (1975)
xref.body: The Ramones were signed by Seymour Stein to Sire Records in 1975 after he discovered them in a Manhattan bar. Other labels refused to sign them because they were considered "too weird," played "too fast," were "too amateurish," and "too funny looking." Mainstream rock radio also rejected them, seeing them as a joke. "back then, nobody wanted to touch the Ramones. They were just too weird. They played too fast. They were too amateurish. And they were too funny looking for all the other labels."

xref.title: External Pressures on the Band (Pre-1977)
xref.body: Before Matlock's departure, the Sex Pistols faced severe external pressures, including constant negative press, numerous canceled gigs, bans from most venues across the UK, and financial instability where no one was getting paid. Johnny Rotten and drummer Paul Cook had already been physically assaulted, contributing to Matlock's decision to leave. "The pistols were under constant attack by the press. Giggs were getting canceled. The group was banned for most venues across the UK. Nobody was getting paid."

xref.title: Michael Stipe's Nervous Breakdown and HIV/AIDS Fears (Leading up to 1985)
xref.body: Michael Stipe experienced a "complete nervous breakdown" leading up to 1985, which went unrecognized by his bandmates, who perceived him as being "impossible." This period was marked by intense fear as a gay man, terrified that his past behaviors would lead to death from AIDS/HIV, a condition not widely discussed at the time. This dread and paranoia, especially during common colds, persisted until he received an anonymous HIV test in 1987. His mental state during this time, coupled with the cold, damp recording conditions in London, notably affected the sound and commercial performance of R.E.M.'s third album, "Fables of the Reconstruction." "Most of the time that I was a pop star, I loved it, but in this period leading up to 1985, I had this complete nervous breakdown and nobody recognized it."

xref.title: Early Viral Online Marketing Campaign (2001)
xref.body: *Machina, the Machines of God* was promoted with a "very cool viral online marketing campaign" in 2001, which was pioneering for its time. Fans were encouraged to decipher the album's weird themes, storylines, and mysteries. However, the campaign was abandoned before it was fully solved or finished. "And there was a very cool viral online marketing campaign that encouraged fans to figure out the weird themes and storylines and mysteries contained in the album and the artwork. Now remember, this was 2001. Nobody was doing this sort of thing back then."

xref.title: Band Estrangement and Public Announcement (2008)
xref.body: During a UK tour in early 2008, no one in the band was speaking with Scott Weiland due to his backsliding drug use. At a Glasgow gig on March 20, 2008, Weiland "announced to the crowd that this was the band's last tour," surprising the rest of the band. "When the road trip got to the UK nobody in the band was speaking with him."

xref.title: Declared Legally Dead (2008)
xref.body: On November 23, 2008, Richie was legally declared dead by his family, who assumed he had taken his own life at the age of 27, though his fate remains officially unknown. "On November 23, 2008, Richie was declared legally dead by his family, having assumed to have taken his own life at that magical and doomed age of, yes, 27. But the bottom line is, nobody knows for sure."

xref.title: MS Diagnosis (April 2017)
xref.body: Art Alexakis began noticing symptoms in 2015, including stumbling and forgetting lyrics, which some mistook for drinking or drug use. He dismissed it as tiredness. After a car crash in April 2017 and a subsequent arm twinge, an MRI, arranged by his daughter, revealed lacerations on his brain indicative of multiple sclerosis. He kept the diagnosis quiet for four years. "Then in April 2017, he was on his way to pick up his daughter at school. It was raining, and he crashed into a jeep. Now nobody was hurt, but then two weeks later, he had a twinge in his arm that he thought was left over from a snowboarding crash or maybe the jeep crash. His daughter set him up with an MRI, and that's when he learned the news. They found lacerations on Art's brain indicative of multiple sclerosis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unexpected Death by Suicide (2017)
xref.body: Chris Cornell's death on May 18th, 2017, came as a "real shock," as no one expected him to die, let alone by suicide. "Nobody expected Chris Cornell to die of anything let alone by his own hand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "A Story Like Mine" – Spoken Word Performance (2018)
xref.body: At the Women's March in New York City in March 2018, Halsey performed a powerful spoken word piece that recounted deeply personal and traumatic experiences of sexual assault and abuse from various stages of her life, and that of her friends, tying it into the broader #MeToo movement. She described a friend's rape at 14 in 2009, her own childhood experience in 2002 by a neighbor's son, a coercive relationship in 2012, and a later assault in 2017 despite believing she was "protected" by her fame. She also revealed performing a show in Chicago while having a miscarriage. The piece emphasized that "nobody is safe" as long as women are alive and acknowledged figures like Ashley, Simone, Gabby, Makayla, Gaga, and Rosario Alli as heroes. "It's Halsey. We're siding up home from a women's march in New York City in March 2018."

xref.title: Aspiration for International Recognition and Box Sets
xref.body: Despite feeling they hadn't "gotten any bigger" in 1999, Sloan continues to record with the long-term goal of accumulating an "enormous body of work." They hope to eventually gain recognition from international publications like Mojo Magazine or Record Collector Magazine, which could lead to a retrospective box set and coffee table book, although they acknowledge the audience might currently be too small without a "huge hit." "Just to have an enormous body of work so that Mojo Magazine finally goes, we are sorry, we never wrote about you guys and you guys are unbelievable and you have all this stuff and nobody knows."

xref.title: Band Name Origin
xref.body: Contrary to the long-standing rumor that R.E.M. chose their name randomly from a dictionary, a 2019 biography asserts that the band's name was derived from the initials of Robert Eugene Miteyard, an obscure photographer from Kentucky. Michael Stipe was reportedly a fan of Miteyard, who signed his prints as REM. "But according to a 2019 biography, REM was actually taken from the initials for Robert Eugene Miteyard, an obscure photographer from Kentucky who signed his prints as REM."

xref.title: CBGB Owner's Reaction to First Gig
xref.body: After their debut 15-minute set at CBGB, the owner expressed skepticism about their appeal but promised to have them back. The band returned the following night and continued to play there frequently, totaling 74 gigs by the end of 1974. "When it was over, the owner said to the band, listen, nobody's going to like you. But you know what, I'll have you back."

xref.title: Engineer's Errors, No Jail Time
xref.body: The engineer central to the Downsview Park stage collapse acknowledged that errors were made in the stage design, but despite this admission and the subsequent recommendations, no one involved in the incident was sent to jail. "The engineer at the center of everything acknowledged that errors were made, but nobody ever went to jail."

xref.title: Famous Anonymous Graffiti Artist
xref.body: Banksy is a famous graffiti artist whose work sells for millions of dollars, yet his identity remains unknown. "Banksy, the famous graffiti artist, who's worked cell for millions of dollars. Nobody knows who Banksy is."

xref.title: First Recording Experience with Tape Handling Error
xref.body: As an engineer at Tapestry Studios, Chris Berkett's first recording session involved a big horn section (possibly for "Geno" by Dexys Midnight Runners). He mistakenly put the 24-track, two-inch tape on backward, resulting in a "wooly" sound, learning from the error without prior instruction. "I realized I put the tape on back to front. No, nobody told me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Five-Year Silence with Tom DeLonge
xref.body: By mid-2008, a significant communication breakdown had occurred between Travis Barker and Tom DeLonge, with Travis noting that he hadn't spoken a word to Tom in five years. This extended silence highlighted the deep rifts within Blink-182, making the prospect of a reunion seem unlikely. "Travis hadn't said a word to Tom in five years or would be the point of getting back together of nobody's talking."

xref.title: Initial Lack of Attention, Later Multi-Platinum Success – Post-Hype Phenomenon
xref.body: Despite receiving great reviews upon its release in April 1991, the Temple of the Dog album was largely ignored by the public. However, once Mookie Blaylock changed its name to Pearl Jam and both Soundgarden and Pearl Jam achieved massive global success, interest in the album exploded, leading it to sell multi-platinum worldwide. "It got great reviews, but nobody paid much attention until Mookie Blaylock changed their name to Pearl Jam and, well, you know, that story."

xref.body: This group, formed by Chris Novoselic with a member of the Meat Puppets and the drummer from Sublime, failed to generate public interest and was finished by 2003. "However, nobody cared, and by 2003 that particular band was finished."

xref.title: Last Project - Kim Deal Solo Record
xref.body: The last record Steve Albini was involved with was Kim Deal's solo record, "Nobody Loves You More," which was released in 2024 and critically acclaimed as one of the year's best alt-rock albums. "And the last record he was part of was the excellent Kim Deal solo record, Nobody Loves You More, which was one of the very best alt rock albums of 2024."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Move to Berlin - Cold War Artistic Hub
xref.body: In an effort to escape the negative influences surrounding him in L.A. and kick his cocaine addiction, Bowie and Iggy Pop moved to Berlin, Germany. During the height of the Cold War, Berlin was a divided city, yet its unique artistic and bohemian culture provided the perfect environment for Bowie's musical evolution, where he immersed himself in German electronic and crude rock sounds. "He and Iggy Pop packed up and left for Berlin. Now Berlin. Nobody went to Berlin. This was the height of the Cold War."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Normalization of Long Hair
xref.body: What began with The Beatles eventually led to long hair on men becoming a completely normal and accepted rock and roll look that persists globally today without a second thought. "Nobody gives it a second thought, and it all begins with the Beatles. They're the ones who made it okay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: North American Label Indifference & UK Interest
xref.body: Initially, no US labels expressed interest in releasing their material, prompting the band to send a demo to Rough Trade Records in the UK, which then agreed to release their *The Modern Age* EP. "Nobody in the US was interested in releasing their stuff, so they sent a demo to rough trade records in the UK, who agreed to release an EP called The Modern Age."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Origins at Ray's Boathouse – Kitchen Work Led to Singing Career
xref.body: In the early 1980s, long before Soundgarden existed, Cornell worked at a Seattle restaurant called Ray's Boathouse, starting as a teenager when his older brother Peter got him a job. He progressed from dishwasher to busboy to sous chef. At the restaurant's annual staff Christmas party, he spontaneously grabbed the microphone from a hired two-man band and launched into "Twist and Shout," astonishing everyone with the power of his voice. The bass player at Ray's Boathouse was Hiro Yamamoto; a maintenance worker named Scott Sundquist (later replaced by Matt Cameron) completed the original 1984 Soundgarden lineup with Kim Thayil on guitar. "Nobody had heard him before and nobody could believe the power of this kid's voice."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneer of Guitar Synthesizers in R&B
xref.body: Peggy Jones distinguished herself through her experiments with guitar synthesizers, which was an uncommon practice in R&B music when she was using them. This innovative approach highlighted her forward-thinking musicality beyond her role as a pioneering female rock guitarist. "She'd later be recognized for her experiments with guitar synthesizers and nobody used those in R&B music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Stage Diving
xref.body: He was one of the very first rock and roll performers to initiate the act of stage diving, a practice that was unheard of before him. "Iggy was one of the first rock and roll performers to stage dive. Nobody had done that before, Iggy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Flop Breakup and Hiatus
xref.body: Following the commercial and critical failure of their 1994 album *Halusagini*, the band broke up, and its members maintained no contact for approximately six years. This period represented a significant hiatus in their collective career. "So the band broke up, and nobody spoke to each other for about six years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

xref.title: Posthumous Recognition as Influential
xref.body: Despite being largely ignored during their active years, The Velvet Underground is now widely regarded as one of the most influential bands of all time, receiving belated credit for their pioneering sound and artistic vision. "And today the Velvet Underground is considered to be one of the most influential bands of all time, yet when they were around, nobody cared."

xref.title: Vogue Magazine Inspiration for Ziggy's Hair
xref.body: After deciding on a new look, David and Angie Bowie searched fashion magazines, eventually finding a version of the desired "new hair thing" in a Vogue advertisement, which served as the blueprint for Ziggy's iconic style. "It was then that neither Bowie or Angie, nobody remembers who, found a version of this new hair thing in an ad in Vogue magazine."
